earlier_mentions.raw_text:
Morgan Stanley’s View on the DeepSeek Shock

1. Semiconductors

While DeepSeek’s success is unlikely to alter semiconductor investment plans significantly, there are several factors to consider.
Feedback from various industry sources consistently indicates that GPU deployment plans remain unaffected.
DeepSeek’s technology is impressive, but major CSPs have not neglected to invest in such technologies.

In fact, much of what we consider groundbreaking—such as training with FP8, multi-token prediction, MLA, custom PTX code, and GRPO reinforcement learning frameworks—either originated with DeepSeek v-2 and DeepSeek’s mathematical model six months ago or can be found in extensive AI research literature.
This underscores the importance of how these technologies are implemented, and DeepSeek provides efficient designs in every respect.

However, given the timing of announcements such as Stargate, Meta’s increased GPU demand forecast for 2025, Microsoft’s reiteration of its $80 billion annual CapEx guidance, and Reliance’s 3GW project in India, those connected to the model ecosystem were likely already aware of most of what DeepSeek was doing.

The long history of algorithmic improvements suggests we should not underestimate the incremental demand driven by cost reductions, advanced functionality, and continued scalability.
NVIDIA has stated that algorithmic efficiency has improved more than 1,000-fold over the past decade, surpassing the performance gains of single-chip inference. In this context, while DeepSeek’s proposal of a 10x reduction in training compute requirements may not significantly impact LTGR (long-term growth rates), the resulting cost savings could accelerate inference adoption and potentially increase demand for inference.

Export controls, however, remain a risk factor.
It is clear that restricting Chinese technology to H20-level performance has not halted China’s development of LLMs. The implications for government policy are unclear at this stage.
Lowering the performance threshold would greatly aid domestic silicon development in China. President Biden’s currently stalled AI restrictions, which aim to limit cluster sizes, would likely have a similar impact. These proposals may also compel other nations capable of supporting China’s AI development to obtain licenses.

Similarly, the performance gap between closed models and open-source ones continues to narrow.
We have highlighted three risks to the AI industry in our bearish outlook (AI remains a key driver, but smaller surprises are expected in 2025). One of these risks is that the number of companies in foundational model development could decline as it becomes increasingly difficult to compete with cheaper open-source options.

DeepSeek’s R1 exacerbates this risk by pressuring the largest spenders in AI to justify larger training runs while allowing others to leverage their work at much lower costs.

2. Internet: Lowering Barriers to Costs Drives Product Innovation and Adoption

DeepSeek’s architecture and pre-training improvements, which enhance cost efficiency, positively impact consumer internet companies seeking to develop new models and LLM-supported products.
The ROIC for GenAI CapEx is expected to increase, and incremental CapEx growth could slow as a result.

Larger companies’ ability to develop more innovative products will increase consumer utility, scalability, and adoption rates.
Given their large capital investments, user bases, and ability to extract and implement DeepSeek’s improvements into their own models, GOOGL, META, and AMZN are poised to benefit the most from these cost savings.

However, with more efficient architectures, smaller companies will also be able to provide GPU-supported products more broadly and at lower costs.
For example, AMZN’s AWS strategy focuses on commoditization at the model layer. AWS integrates third-party models and provides access through tools like Bedrock, enabling customers to build applications.

If DeepSeek’s contributions to democratizing model building (reducing required costs and compute) further commoditize models, AWS could benefit as an aggregator.

3. Software: Reducing AI Deployment Costs for Software Providers

Algorithmic efficiency gains at the model layer positively impact enterprise software.
More cost-efficient models are reducing the “GenAI deployment costs” for the broader software ecosystem, and the companies we cover are primarily building solutions around these models.

These efficiency improvements are not surprising to the software ecosystem. Most software companies believe that lower deployment costs lead to higher utilization (the Jevons paradox) and have already actively worked to lower these costs.

Microsoft recently focused on its “Phi” small language model (SML) strategy, with the Phi-4 14B model delivering benchmark results comparable to Llama-3.3 70B.

ServiceNow partnered with Nvidia to use custom domain-specific language models to execute inference more cost-effectively.

Snowflake trained Arctic 17B LLM with a $2 million training compute budget, achieving comparable performance to other enterprise benchmarks and best-in-class SQL performance.

Elastic developed the Elastic Learned Sparse EncodeR (ELSER) to lower the cost of semantic search for AI applications.

4. Energy

Regarding stocks exposed to the growth of AI power infrastructure in the U.S., significant capital expenditures are expected to continue.
Key considerations include:
1. An analysis of the U.S. data center pipeline indicates that most of the known pipeline is for AI inference and non-AI use cases rather than AI training.
2. The “Powering GenAI Models” analysis suggests that computing costs could drop by ~90% over the next six years. As AI adoption increases, the Jevons paradox could lead to rapidly growing demand for AI computing.
3. Discussions with companies suggest that substantial AI infrastructure spending is currently happening in the U.S. (Stargate being one of the most prominent projects we anticipate).
4. After the recent sell-off, many stocks exposed to U.S. AI infrastructure growth are still undervalued and not fully pricing in AI growth.

5. IT Hardware: The Focus of AI in IT Hardware and Apple’s Position

Last weekend’s DeepSeek news raised many unanswered questions (particularly regarding total compute costs and final training runs). Still, concerns about AI-related stocks’ long-term ripple effects are evident, especially for DELL (AI infrastructure) and STX (HDD), which may be the most impacted.

We believe $AAPL could emerge as a relative winner in this debate:

1. Apple’s AI ambitions are primarily focused on feature-specific, on-device small LLMs rather than large frontier models, meaning its AI investments are far less visible than those of its peers.

Consequently, Apple’s annual CapEx ($9.4 billion for FY24) is about 1/20th of the combined CapEx of U.S. Tier 1 hyperscalers. If the market overemphasizes CapEx ROI, Apple faces a much lower bar to generate attractive returns (i.e., less risk).

2. As DeepSeek has demonstrated, reduced memory requirements for inference make “Edge AI” much more feasible, aligning with Apple’s core GenAI ambitions.

3. In a world where consumer LLMs are commoditized, distribution platforms become key assets, and Apple owns arguably the most valuable consumer tech distribution platform in existence.

6. Embodied AI/Tesla: Advancements in GenAI Training Drive Embodied AI

In addition to the potential applications and acceleration of robotics training, we anticipate increasing attention on physical AI as growth in the digital AI narrative becomes less obvious and investors seek executable stories elsewhere.

In other words, as companies in the digital AI space become less reliant on double-digit returns, the early-stage opportunities in embodied AI—ranging from humanoids to eVTOL, AMRs, and AVs—are expected to appear increasingly attractive.

From a geopolitical perspective, autonomous vehicles currently operate in several cities at 25% of traditional taxi costs, supported by government policies encouraging innovation and supply chains for low-cost local production components. These developments once again highlight China’s achievements in embodied AI.

Faced with China’s advancements, the U.S.’s biggest geopolitical rival in all areas of AI, policymakers are expected to pay greater attention to fostering competitive progress among U.S. companies in this space.
$NVDA

According to South Korean media reports, Apple is set to equip the iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max, scheduled for release in the second half of this year, with 12GB of mobile DRAM. The iPhone lineup consists of four models—two standard and two Pro models—and the higher-end Pro and Pro Max will be the first to adopt 12GB memory.

This marks the first time Apple is adopting 12GB DRAM in its iPhones. After equipping the iPhone 15 Pro with 8GB DRAM in 2023, Apple has maintained 8GB memory through the iPhone 16 series. This upgrade, coming after two years, is interpreted as a move to enhance DRAM capacity in response to AI.

Smartphones are now being redefined by AI. They assist with not only photo editing but also document organization and translation. To implement such AI features on smartphones, high-performance system semiconductors like application processors (APs) are essential, but so is increased memory. Large volumes of data must be processed quickly to deliver AI services on demand.

Apple introduced its proprietary AI, “Apple Intelligence,” last year and suggested that at least 8GB of memory is required to operate it. As AI utilization expands, Apple has judged that even greater memory is needed, leading to the decision to equip the Pro models with 12GB.

The 12GB memory for the iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max is reportedly being supplied by Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix, and Micron. In particular, Samsung is said to be responsible for 70% of total demand. Considering Apple typically sells around 100 million new iPhones in the year following release, Samsung would be supplying about 70 million units. The remaining 30% is being split between SK Hynix and Micron.

Apple’s expansion of iPhone memory signals the full-fledged arrival of AI in the smartphone market and foreshadows a major shift in DRAM demand in the mobile sector, following the server and data center markets.

According to market research firm Counterpoint Research, shipments of AI phones this year are projected to surpass 405 million units, a 68% increase from last year. As AI phones increase, so does memory capacity, resulting in market growth.

Additionally, as “on-device AI,” where AI runs directly on the smartphone, continues to develop, the data processing speed of mobile DRAM must also improve—driving the development of new technologies.

Indeed, there are emerging efforts to stack DRAM in mobile devices, similar to high-bandwidth memory (HBM), to enhance performance.

In their Q1 earnings calls, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix both stated, “Smartphones will continue to drive high-performance memory demand due to the integration of AI models like small language models (Small LLMs).”

As more AI phones require large-capacity memory, the profitability of the memory industry improves. On average, 12GB RAM is about 50% more expensive than 8GB RAM.

Another industry insider commented, “The expansion of large-capacity DRAM demand is also expected to benefit the substrate industry,” adding, “Major substrate manufacturers have already fully entered the 12GB RAM supply chain.”

Samsung Electronics is reportedly working with Samsung Electro-Mechanics, SK Hynix with LG Innotek, and Micron with Japan’s Shinko Electric Industries to produce 12GB mobile DRAM for iPhones.

BofA) Expert Call with Former Intel Lithography and Foundry Executive

Yesterday, we hosted an expert call with Klaus Shuegraf, currently VP at Photonic and formerly Director of Lithography Sourcing and VP of Foundry Strategy & Planning at Intel.

1. EUV Source Power and Increasing Lithographic Intensity Expected to Continue

Shuegraf acknowledged that the transition from N3 to N2 nodes does not significantly shrink feature sizes due to the Gate-All-Around (GAA) structure. However, he projected that lithographic intensity will continue to increase for nodes beyond that. He expressed confidence in ASML achieving 1000W source power from the current 600W, but noted that reaching 1500W would approach technical limitations.

2. 18A Node Outlook and High-NA Adoption Timing

In line with industry trends, Shuegraf stated that Intel must first prove the viability of its 18A node through its own products before attracting potential customers such as AVGO (Broadcom), NVDA (Nvidia), and AAPL (Apple M-series). He predicted that 2026 would be the mainstream ramp-up period for 18A, which would be about one year behind TSMC’s 2nm node production schedule. Regarding High-NA EUV, he noted that TSMC’s full adoption would likely be in the late 2020s, as it will take time for ASML to scale up production capacity.

3. Potential Expansion of EUV Adoption in DRAM

Shuegraf suggested that if leading HBM suppliers adopt EUV, it could drive broader EUV adoption across the DRAM industry. This is due to trends such as AI PCs and advanced packaging making DRAM a more specialized, rather than purely commoditized, product segment. While some customers may be able to maintain current lithographic intensity levels through 4F2 architecture, others are expected to adopt additional litho layers alongside 4F2.

4. Additional Notes on China and ALD

(A) Regarding China’s development of EUV using DPP (Discharge Produced Plasma), Shuegraf acknowledged that for AI use cases, high wafer throughput is not always essential. However, he commented that DPP is economically inefficient and presents challenges in supply availability.

(B) On the topic of ALD (Atomic Layer Deposition), he emphasized that ASMI remains the leading player due to its position as the only vertically integrated vendor with an in-house chemical supply chain.

Was the first to talk about $AXTI in relation to photonics BOM/supply chains:

$IQE is very interesting too as one of the only Western suppliers. 

Basically if you look at photonics flow on $GOOGL TPU/hyperscaler ASICs kinda looks like this (very likely, but undisclosed): 

Optical Transceivers (highest BOM):

Lumentum/Cloud Light:
~ Vital / $AXTI-> $AXTI/Sumitomo/JX -> $IQE (Epi-Wafers) -> $LITE / Cloud Light -> $FN (Contract Manufacturing) -> $GOOGL TPU

Merhcant optical supply chain:

~ Vital / $AXTI -> $AXTI / Sumitomo / JX  -> → $LITE / $AVGO / $COHR (EML) + $MRVL / $MTSI / Semtech -> Innolight/Eoptolink -> $GOOGL 

So if you want moonshot-type photonics BOM / price-hikes stocks deeper upstream in the photonics BOM: $AXTI, $IQE and your way to go. 

$AXTI had terrible fundamentals before but the recent Northland fundraising round cemented its run. 

$IQE has terrible fundamentals now (Net debt £23.5 million) but is probably one of the most critical parts of the supply chain. If they manage to sell their Taiwan operations, wouldn't be surprised if it went up quite a bit just from their inp business. 

There's £18m convertible notes (which is basically nothing), then there's 120 to 154m new shares (~12% to 15%), which is also kinda nothing relative to current size. 

On the other hand, others $LITE and Innolight are probably more established. 

TLDR:

$IQE -> seems critical to Western supply chains, $130MC. Net debt, if they sell Taiwan business -> strong re-rating or they might just dilute you anyway. 

But if the Taiwan business fails to be sold, probably expect to be diluted to oblivion like Wolfspeed. So huge, huge, risk ad do you own research into risks. 

But $AXTI and $IQE might are personally interesting to me (I do own $IQE).

A Guide by Serenity: 

How to Cripple the Western Hyperscaler buildout with just $170m.

Just take over Nippon Chemical (4092) with $169m!

For InP substrates, you need: Indium and High Purity Phosphorus.

Thought $AXTI was a bottleneck? NCI is the bottleneck of the bottleneck.

NCI is actually the leader of the high purity red phosphorus chokepoint holding 26-27% of the market share (Rasa has less share, then the rest is China). 

And they export to $AXTI, Sumitomo, JX that need it to make InP substrates. 
 So… if you have $160m to spend to acquire NCI (plus Rasa as smaller capacity), you can remove the leading Western world’s production of 6N/7N red phosphorus needed to make InP substrates!

And without InP substrates: no photonics. 

Fun fact: China’s tech companies would get pretty disrupted with it too by NCI.  

For $AXTI, the mapping/reliance is actually pretty interesting: 

- AXT's Tongmei outlined its structural reliance on importing high-purity precursor materials from Japan on their STAR Market listing
 - WITS data showing ~$460/kg high-purity phosphorus flowing from Japan into China

So they secretly do depend on NCI.
 China does have capacity like Wylton Chemical, Qin Xi New Materials, Jinding Electronics, and Chuxiong Chuanzhi, Guizhou Wylton Jinglin Electronic Materials as well.

However, they’re all smaller players so can’t make up for high purity red phosphorus capacity provided by NCI for InP substrate production at scale. 

$LITE CEO already said inp substrates keeps him up at night. 

So now with NCI, you can give the guy permanent insomnia? 

For just $169M. 

So here's what the supply chain looks like:

-> DGC phosphate rock mine and ships it to NCI
-> NCI refines Yellow Phosphorus into High Purity Red Phosphorus 
->  Sumitomo / JX / AXT melt the Red Phosphorus with Indium to grow InP Substrates
-> $COHR / $LITE fab InP substrates into Lasers
-> Innolight/Fabrinet package them into 800G/1.6T transceivers
-> $NVDA / $GOOGL use them for ASIC/GPU clusters. 
 And basically, the entire West depends on NCI to make InP substrates for photonics.

So you’d probably run into regulatory problems eg. FEFTA if you bought the company and hiked prices 15000% (like government seizing back the company once they realize)… 

Maybe 30-50% hikes is possible to compress fwd p/e? But very likely wont end up like $AXTI.  
Regardless, this company is a massive, massive national security risk priced at ~$160m. 

As for fundamentals, they’re trading at .54 book value and a forward P/E of 11.4 so it’s probably undervalued anyway. 

TLDR:

->  Is it the next $AXTI? No. 

-> Is it an unknown structural bottleneck + critical vulnerability of the Western hyperscaler buildout with photonics? Yes.

-> Is there still room for re-rating? 

Just reverting to Book Value of 1 is immediate 80-85% upside. Maybe more if you give it multiples past 11 fwd p/e.

Photonics is the newest supercycle (maybe H1 into H2 2025 was the start).

Then there's many different architectural changes in each supercycle:

-> $LITE, $COHR, Innolight, $AXTI and these names led the first 

I did a thesis post on mentioning all four of them as the largest beneficiaries (all are up 500-1000% 1Y)

-> $AAOI, $JBL and others types of names are benefit immensely as the transitional bridge (eg. 1.6T pluggable)

Of course, $LITE does everything. $AXTI will be used for everything. 

But the amount of pure play exposure for each architectural shift in each mini supercycle is different.

There's probably still 50%+ with $LITE and $COHR. And you're a little on the "late" side of things. 

But you're extremely early to new architecture generations. 

What I'm trying to do is point regular retail investors into the direction of new gold mines for free. 

Before institutions figure out sooner or later by paying $20k for equity research reports.

earlier_mentions.raw_text:
Here's a deeper look into $IQE ($179M):

IQE's hidden InP optionality versus LandMark's $3.5B valuation. And the $IREN / $CRWV "miner" pivot to photonics: 

Before I did a high-level shower thought overview eg. $AXTI -> $IQE -> $LITE -> $GOOGL TPUs, but this is slightly more DD. 

Basically: IQE is the largest independent merchant compound semi epitaxial foundry in the world by reactor count and physical capacity. 

However, it's trading at distressed valuations because it's burdened by a low-margin legacy wireless business, and near-term liquidity constraints. 

LandMark Optoelectronics (TPEX: 3081) is the closest comparison. As a pure-play proxy for AI InP demand in the 800G and 1.6T optical interconnect market, LandMark commands a ~$3.8B billion market cap with large premiums in comparison to $IQE which is trading at a $175M MC. 

But if you look deeper at the physical hardware, the disconnect is pretty fascinating:

LandMark's operational scale is physically limited. They only operate around 27 to 30 Metal-Organic Chemical Vapor Deposition (MOCVD) reactors out of a single campus in Taiwan per some estimates. 

IQE, by stark contrast, possesses well over 100+ MOCVD and MBE systems globally. 

The underlying replacement value and structural capacity of IQE’s photonics asset base looks to vastly exceeds its current public market valuation.

Kind of like if a Bitcoin miner has 3GW capacity, vs 750 MW, there's large optionality to monetize it if they convert it.  

And we're seeing an transceiver bottleneck too: 

-> The downstream demand for optical transceivers is experiencing unprecedented acceleration.

-> Extreme demand, from $GOOGL, $MSFT, $AMZN and others flow directly up the hardware supply chain.

This puts immense pressure on transceiver integrators like Innolight, optical component manufacturers like $COHR, $LITE, and $AVGO, and ultimately, the merchant epitaxial foundries that grow the raw epiwafers required for the foundational laser chips. 

And since other players are hitting a physical capacity ceiling, vertically integrated players like $COHR are capped out, hyperscalers and module makers are desperate for alternative capacity in players like $IQE

And..

Hidden entirely beneath IQE's consolidated corporate lines is a massive fleet of Aixtron AIX 2800G4-TM reactors. 

These are natively dual-capable (GaAs/InP) and can be repurposed for InP production at a relatively modest cost ($500K-$1.5M per reactor) but take few months or year to refactor. And obviously qualification and yield risk added to execution (similar to Bitcoin miners doing software orchestration to GPUs like $CRWV). 

But still,  IQE has the capacity kinda like $IREN or Bitcoin miners that pivoted to HPC. And LandMark is proof of the valuation pure play exposure brings. 

The Major Question..  Unlocking Trapped Value:

While IQE generates significantly higher top-line revenue than LandMark, it's priced ($175M MC) for bankruptcy because of its gross debt of 45M. 

But the debt looks like pennies to hyperscalers:

The explicit, stated goal of their ongoing Lazard-advised strategic review is to definitively conclude the sale of IQE Taiwan (their legacy GaAs wireless business) and utilize the proceeds to completely and permanently extinguish the parent company's restrictive debt profile.

Once again their convertible loan notes is a norminal face value of £21.2 million, for proceeds of £18 million for the company. Then they're net debt, £23.5 million. 

-> The immediate debt burden requiring clearance: £23.5M HSBC facility + £21.2M CLN = ~£45M.

Assuming a highly sale price for the IQE Taiwan unit of between £100 million and £150 millio (not guaranteed), IQE would net £50 million to £100 million in surplus cash after becoming completely debt-free. 

However, RF GaAs is not currently "hot", so in a distressed asset sale it might only be £50M to £60M, which gives it enough room to clear debt alone and little cushion room. 

The Geopolitical Pivot:

Once debt-free, IQE can shift its massive, currently underutilized manufacturing capacity in places like North Carolina and Wales toward the InP epiwafer market for datacenters.

It creates a fully capitalized, purely Western-based supply chain for the most critical bottleneck in photonics, eliminating more dependency on Asia at a time when the US and UK are heavily prioritizing domestic semiconductor infrastructure.

Basically, just given the amount of raw assets $IQE has:

 -> Successfully selling off their Taiwan business wipes out the going-concern risks, clears all debt, and leaves them to monetize their 6-inch inp epiwafer tech directly for the Tier 1 optical transceiver players.

It's a deep asset value trade on a successful restructuring to unlock trapped value. And a currently well-known supplier for optical networking for hyperscalers (so not a science project). 

Downside risks are excessive dilution and failure to restructure. But given it's geopolitical importance to Western supply chains and hyperscaler supply chains, it seems to have more cushion. 

I personally decided to enter this long as a massive potential turnaround. But again, it's not for everyone and it's extremely high risk. 

TLDR:

-> IQE is priced like a distressed RF supplier.
-> It owns real photonics-capable infrastructure. 
-> If gross 41M debt is removed and management reallocates capex toward InP, the equity could rerate materially.
-> Restructuring + capacity optionality trade with extreme risk but extreme upside. 

Closest comparison is Bitcoin miners like $IREN or $CIFR that pivot their GW capacity to AI HPC. They have a ton of physical hardware (GW capacity), and need funds to pivot (either through sale of Taiwan business or dilution). 

It's an optimistic trade I took they can do it (with wiggle room like $INTC given their geopolitical importance to the West). 

The downside is extreme dilution, which is always a possibility (meaning your equity gets wiped out to 0 to clear their debts or to help them refactor). 

I just found that 45M gross debt (14.4% of float + debt) wasn't the most and management was looking to clear that through asset sales rather than dilution to shareholders. 

Just wanted to publish deeper breakdown and more risks of this very binary **high risk**, but potentially high upside trade.

So here's the napkin math I did on Nextronics (8147) when I went long.

They're the $NVDA CPO supplier for CPO connectors and cage thermal modules.

And I modeled around 2 FWD p/e for 2028, which is why I think risk-reward is very compelling for a potential 10x rerating to ~$2B+ MC in 2028.

Just for their CPO exposure:

-> CPO connector runs roughly $15 to $25
-> ELS thermal cages, maybe ~$50 from est.

18 units per switch: 18x50 = ~$900
CPO Connectors: 72 Optical Engines per switch 72 x $15 = $1,080
(If $NVDA scales their Spectrum-X switch, it goes to $1,920 for CPO connectors).

rows.raw_text:
I just realized Boston Dynamics CEO shared the same sentiment:

“Robotics is next. America’s next 250 years will be built by robots”.

However, currently China accounts for 54%+ of all global robotics deployments.

- calls for Internet scaleable database of physical world (kinda got reminded of Niantic that has a huge dataset from Pokemon Go)

- dedicated National robotics strategy to compete against China’s leadership in this space

-  ISO + regulation for robotics safety 

This is all high level:

But my prioritize thought process is how do we support and scale a Made in USA supply chain for robotics/humanoids?

I’ve been hammering home rare earths for the longest time, that the US isn’t doing enough to subsidize or scale this industry.

JP Morgan Report on DeepSeek

Yesterday, we saw the market experience significant volatility as it reflected the following factors: 1) TXN (-7.5%) earnings and renewed concerns around analog, 2) META (+1.7%) surprising CAPEX increase, and 3) ongoing worries related to CPOs (ALAB -6.6%; COHR -6.9%). However, 95% of the questions we received were about the Chinese AI company DeepSeek, particularly regarding how they managed to develop state-of-the-art models on a modest budget, raising questions about the billions being poured into cutting-edge AI CAPEX (as reflected in NVDA -3% and VRT -5.2% today).

We believe these concerns are overblown and would like to share why. However, since this discussion is unlikely to be resolved quickly, we are interested in hearing your thoughts and counterpoints.

DeepSeek is a two-year-old AI R&D venture startup based in Hangzhou, China, fully funded and operated by High-Flyer, a leading Chinese quant fund. High-Flyer was founded in 2015 by friends from the prestigious Zhejiang University, aiming to use machine learning for stock trading. In 2023, they spun off this independent research division to develop highly efficient, state-of-the-art AI models using open-source models (you can find their company profile and interviews with their founders here). DeepSeek’s stated goal is to pursue AGI rather than application development or monetization, and its founder, Liang Wenfeng, is known as a “maverick.”

DeepSeek quickly gained attention with its DeepSeek-V2, R1 Lite, and V3 models. The release of R1 Lite in late November was particularly notable for outperforming OpenAI’s o1 model in several benchmarks as a test-time scaling model. This Monday, DeepSeek announced its test-time models R1 and R1-Zero, which have shown competitiveness against OpenAI’s test-time models. The R1 model, which can be experienced here, demonstrates impressive capabilities in explaining the process of understanding user intent and generating responses. Meanwhile, R1-Zero is a unique model trained entirely without supervised fine-tuning.

What has drawn the most attention, however, are DeepSeek’s research papers and the efficiency of its models. It is unclear to what extent DeepSeek is utilizing High-Flyer’s approximately 50,000 Hopper GPUs (a cluster comparable in size to the one OpenAI is rumored to be using for GPT-5 training). What is evident, though, is that they are dramatically reducing costs (for example, they claim that the inference cost of the V2 model is 1/7th that of GPT-4 Turbo). This week, their disruptive (but not entirely new) assertion, which has begun to impact U.S. AI companies, is that “more investment does not necessarily equate to more innovation.” Liang Wenfeng stated, “At present, we see no new approaches, but big companies do not hold a clear advantage. While they have existing customers, their cash flow businesses can become burdensome and make them vulnerable to innovation at any time.” Regarding the delay in GPT-5’s release, he added, “OpenAI is not a god and does not need to always remain at the forefront.”

SemiAnalysis’ Dylan Patel has been pointing this out since June. This does not signify the end of scaling, the end of needing more computing power, or that the most capital-intensive player won’t win (remember Mark Zuckerberg announced a sharp increase in AI CAPEX yesterday). Instead, it suggests that competitors across the Pacific have been forced to pursue efficiency due to export restrictions: “DeepSeek V2 demonstrated astonishing training efficiency, achieving better model performance than other open models with 1/5th the computing power of Meta’s Llama 3 70B. For context, training DeepSeek V2 required only 1/20th the FLOPs of GPT-4, while delivering comparable performance.” If DeepSeek can reduce inference costs, others will have to follow suit, and over time, demand may offset this trend.

There are several recent Substack articles about DeepSeek. In the coming weeks, we will learn more about how this company’s success in cost reduction might reshape the outlook for the AI industry (and the trajectory of chip demand for inference).

earlier_mentions.raw_text:
Morgan Stanley’s View on the DeepSeek Shock

1. Semiconductors

While DeepSeek’s success is unlikely to alter semiconductor investment plans significantly, there are several factors to consider.
Feedback from various industry sources consistently indicates that GPU deployment plans remain unaffected.
DeepSeek’s technology is impressive, but major CSPs have not neglected to invest in such technologies.

In fact, much of what we consider groundbreaking—such as training with FP8, multi-token prediction, MLA, custom PTX code, and GRPO reinforcement learning frameworks—either originated with DeepSeek v-2 and DeepSeek’s mathematical model six months ago or can be found in extensive AI research literature.
This underscores the importance of how these technologies are implemented, and DeepSeek provides efficient designs in every respect.

However, given the timing of announcements such as Stargate, Meta’s increased GPU demand forecast for 2025, Microsoft’s reiteration of its $80 billion annual CapEx guidance, and Reliance’s 3GW project in India, those connected to the model ecosystem were likely already aware of most of what DeepSeek was doing.

The long history of algorithmic improvements suggests we should not underestimate the incremental demand driven by cost reductions, advanced functionality, and continued scalability.
NVIDIA has stated that algorithmic efficiency has improved more than 1,000-fold over the past decade, surpassing the performance gains of single-chip inference. In this context, while DeepSeek’s proposal of a 10x reduction in training compute requirements may not significantly impact LTGR (long-term growth rates), the resulting cost savings could accelerate inference adoption and potentially increase demand for inference.

Export controls, however, remain a risk factor.
It is clear that restricting Chinese technology to H20-level performance has not halted China’s development of LLMs. The implications for government policy are unclear at this stage.
Lowering the performance threshold would greatly aid domestic silicon development in China. President Biden’s currently stalled AI restrictions, which aim to limit cluster sizes, would likely have a similar impact. These proposals may also compel other nations capable of supporting China’s AI development to obtain licenses.

Similarly, the performance gap between closed models and open-source ones continues to narrow.
We have highlighted three risks to the AI industry in our bearish outlook (AI remains a key driver, but smaller surprises are expected in 2025). One of these risks is that the number of companies in foundational model development could decline as it becomes increasingly difficult to compete with cheaper open-source options.

DeepSeek’s R1 exacerbates this risk by pressuring the largest spenders in AI to justify larger training runs while allowing others to leverage their work at much lower costs.

2. Internet: Lowering Barriers to Costs Drives Product Innovation and Adoption

DeepSeek’s architecture and pre-training improvements, which enhance cost efficiency, positively impact consumer internet companies seeking to develop new models and LLM-supported products.
The ROIC for GenAI CapEx is expected to increase, and incremental CapEx growth could slow as a result.

Larger companies’ ability to develop more innovative products will increase consumer utility, scalability, and adoption rates.
Given their large capital investments, user bases, and ability to extract and implement DeepSeek’s improvements into their own models, GOOGL, META, and AMZN are poised to benefit the most from these cost savings.

However, with more efficient architectures, smaller companies will also be able to provide GPU-supported products more broadly and at lower costs.
For example, AMZN’s AWS strategy focuses on commoditization at the model layer. AWS integrates third-party models and provides access through tools like Bedrock, enabling customers to build applications.

If DeepSeek’s contributions to democratizing model building (reducing required costs and compute) further commoditize models, AWS could benefit as an aggregator.

3. Software: Reducing AI Deployment Costs for Software Providers

Algorithmic efficiency gains at the model layer positively impact enterprise software.
More cost-efficient models are reducing the “GenAI deployment costs” for the broader software ecosystem, and the companies we cover are primarily building solutions around these models.

These efficiency improvements are not surprising to the software ecosystem. Most software companies believe that lower deployment costs lead to higher utilization (the Jevons paradox) and have already actively worked to lower these costs.

Microsoft recently focused on its “Phi” small language model (SML) strategy, with the Phi-4 14B model delivering benchmark results comparable to Llama-3.3 70B.

ServiceNow partnered with Nvidia to use custom domain-specific language models to execute inference more cost-effectively.

Snowflake trained Arctic 17B LLM with a $2 million training compute budget, achieving comparable performance to other enterprise benchmarks and best-in-class SQL performance.

Elastic developed the Elastic Learned Sparse EncodeR (ELSER) to lower the cost of semantic search for AI applications.

4. Energy

Regarding stocks exposed to the growth of AI power infrastructure in the U.S., significant capital expenditures are expected to continue.
Key considerations include:
1. An analysis of the U.S. data center pipeline indicates that most of the known pipeline is for AI inference and non-AI use cases rather than AI training.
2. The “Powering GenAI Models” analysis suggests that computing costs could drop by ~90% over the next six years. As AI adoption increases, the Jevons paradox could lead to rapidly growing demand for AI computing.
3. Discussions with companies suggest that substantial AI infrastructure spending is currently happening in the U.S. (Stargate being one of the most prominent projects we anticipate).
4. After the recent sell-off, many stocks exposed to U.S. AI infrastructure growth are still undervalued and not fully pricing in AI growth.

5. IT Hardware: The Focus of AI in IT Hardware and Apple’s Position

Last weekend’s DeepSeek news raised many unanswered questions (particularly regarding total compute costs and final training runs). Still, concerns about AI-related stocks’ long-term ripple effects are evident, especially for DELL (AI infrastructure) and STX (HDD), which may be the most impacted.

We believe $AAPL could emerge as a relative winner in this debate:

1. Apple’s AI ambitions are primarily focused on feature-specific, on-device small LLMs rather than large frontier models, meaning its AI investments are far less visible than those of its peers.

Consequently, Apple’s annual CapEx ($9.4 billion for FY24) is about 1/20th of the combined CapEx of U.S. Tier 1 hyperscalers. If the market overemphasizes CapEx ROI, Apple faces a much lower bar to generate attractive returns (i.e., less risk).

2. As DeepSeek has demonstrated, reduced memory requirements for inference make “Edge AI” much more feasible, aligning with Apple’s core GenAI ambitions.

3. In a world where consumer LLMs are commoditized, distribution platforms become key assets, and Apple owns arguably the most valuable consumer tech distribution platform in existence.

6. Embodied AI/Tesla: Advancements in GenAI Training Drive Embodied AI

In addition to the potential applications and acceleration of robotics training, we anticipate increasing attention on physical AI as growth in the digital AI narrative becomes less obvious and investors seek executable stories elsewhere.

In other words, as companies in the digital AI space become less reliant on double-digit returns, the early-stage opportunities in embodied AI—ranging from humanoids to eVTOL, AMRs, and AVs—are expected to appear increasingly attractive.

From a geopolitical perspective, autonomous vehicles currently operate in several cities at 25% of traditional taxi costs, supported by government policies encouraging innovation and supply chains for low-cost local production components. These developments once again highlight China’s achievements in embodied AI.

Faced with China’s advancements, the U.S.’s biggest geopolitical rival in all areas of AI, policymakers are expected to pay greater attention to fostering competitive progress among U.S. companies in this space.

Rising macro risks and AI reality check for 2H25F- Nomura

GB200 bottlenecks largely behind us, but demand reality checks amid rising macro risks will be key for 2H25F Server market – we lower our 2025F AI server revenue assumption to reflect the slowerthan-expected rack output of GB200 in 1Q25, although the weakness is well-expected. While in Feb 2025 we had observed an improving yield rate of GB200 for final testing , the actual final rack ramp-ups in 1Q25 disappointed, likely due to the labor-intensive process for cable wiring and final assembly, inefficient testing processes, movement of production locations (from Mexico or Taiwan to the US) on potential tariff concerns, and the slow learning curve at US production sites. As a result, the actual GB200 rack shipments were below 1,000 racks in 1Q25 (based on our supply-chain checks), lower than our original expectation of about 3,000 racks.

Furthermore, the sudden design change of GB300 compute tray from Cordelia architecture to GB200’s Bianca architecture in early April could cause some concerns of delay on GB300 and a longer transitional period between GB200 and GB300. Hence, we estimate the final GB200/300 rack shipments will reach ~20k units in 2025F (we had previously estimated 28-30k units), considering the extremely low shipments YTD and the potential GB300 delay. Our new GB rack number (20k) for 2025F implies <1k, 5-6k, 8k, 6k units in 1Q, 2Q, 3Q, and 4Q25F, respectively. Our estimates are higher than the recent bearish sell-side forecasts (source: Bloomberg) of 15-20k, but roughly in line with the mid-range Bloomberg consensus estimates. We forecast a significant jump in GB200 rack shipments in 2Q25F (from <1k in 1Q25F to 5-6k in 2Q25F), as we observe ODMs have gradually ramped up the learning curve for final rack assembly and testing in April-May, and that monthly output will likely rise 3-4x by May-June, vs March. With the design changes of GB300, we lower our assumptions on GB rack shipments for 4Q25F, due to the potential transition from GB200 to GB300. 

However, GB200/300 demand in 2H25 will be key. So far, CSPs (Cloud Service Providers) have not placed large firm orders (~3k/3-4k in 1Q/2Q25F only, on our estimates) for GB200/300, in part due to the very few final product deliveries over the past few months and the frequent changes of nVidia’s product roadmap and designs. We believe the real demand in 1H25F will come in higher than the firm order levels, and with eased bottlenecks and designs locking down, we see real demand for GB200, and hopefully GB300, surfacing in 2H25F. However, macro risks are on the rise in 2H25F given Trump’s intention to implement high tariffs. Hence, at this juncture, it is difficult to have clear visibility on real demand for nVidia’s AI servers (as well as for global tech products) in 2H25F.

We lower our global AI server revenue estimates by 4%/13% for 2025/26F to reflect the slowed ramp-up of GB200 in 1H25, potential delay of GB300, and rising macro uncertainties. We now forecast global server revenue growth of 44%/11% y-y for 2025F/26F (Fig. 1 ) (vs prior 46%/22% y-y for 2025F/26F ), with AI server revenue growth rate at 69%/18% y-y in 2025F/26F (previously 75%/31% y-y). 

We raise our general server revenue by 3% for 2025F, but cut by 4% for 2026F, as we observe strong restocking and early pull-in ahead of the new tariff policy from the US in 1H25F, but we are cautious on a potential demand slowdown by 4Q25-2026F due to macro demand risks. As such, our general server revenue estimate is growth of 14% in 2025F (vs prior 10%), but a decline of 3% in 2026F (vs prior up 4%). 

Updates on GB300 design change and potential push-out of single-die B300 (for NVL16 HGX) 

We highlighted on 10 April that the design of the GB300 compute tray (Cordelia architecture) might change back to the GB200 Bianca architecture , because the GPU OAM (OCP [Open Compute Project] accelerator module) connection to the PCB (through LGA sockets) has encountered transmission issues and this issue could take a longer time to resolve, potentially casting uncertainty over the yield rate in later stages even if mass production is on time. We think leveraging the existing Bianca design (which yield rate has been stable), without changing components on the board, and only replacing B200 GPU by B300 GPU could help shorten the time to market.

Under the condition of not changing the design and components on the Bianca board, completing the testing process (especially connecting to new CX8, vs prior CX7) and modifying the peripheral power delivery board design (PDB, as the B300 requires higher power (1400W) than B200 (1200W)) would be the next process. Therefore, nVidia is still targeting to start mass production of the new Bianca GB300 module by the end of June (same schedule as original Cordelia GB300). However, we are not sure whether there would be unexpected challenges for such change, and some CSPs might prefer to buy more GB200 in 3Q25F, in case GB300 runs into further complications. Given the short notice, even if Bianca GB300 module can be produced on time, we think CSPs still require some time for tailor-made modifications. Hence, we expect a product transition impact in 4Q25F, if the ramp-up of GB300 racks for larger CSPs is delayed from 4Q25 to 1Q26.

Meanwhile, there is still no clarity on the demand and the product roadmap of HGX products (NVL8 B200 or B300, or single-die B300 NVL16). nVidia has been planning for single-die B300 NVL16 HGX to replace B200 (dual GPU die) NVL8 HGX. However, the new HGX NVL16 or NVL8 based on B300 might also encounter similar socket connection issues. We highlight that the supply chain is still working to resolve the socket connection issue for HGX and this could delay the product launch. In addition, the development of single-die B300 is now in the ‘pending’ stage again (i.e., originally it was B300A based on CoWoS-S for products like GB300A (cancelled), and it was later changed to CoWoS-L in January (after nVidia cut TSMC’s CoWoS-S ) mainly for HGX NVL16).

Given such changes and the unclear roadmap for HGX, we revise our GB and HGX mix forecasts for 2025F/2026F to 66%/69% and 34%/31% (Fig. 1 ) , from 52%/50% and 48%/50%, respectively.

If there is more CoWoS cut (highly likely), with downstream output ramping up, the gap between CoWoS supply and demand could narrow by late-2025F In our February update, we already considered the potential of nVidia’s CoWoS-S cut in mid-January , but we noted that nVidia lowered its CoWoS-L in March (likely to cancel the overbooking in CoWoS-L [which exceeded its booking in front-end foundry] and the potential push-out of the single-die B300).

However, despite the lowered CoWoS supply, the gap between nVidia’s CoWoS-based IC supply and nVidia’s sell-out and the gap between nVidia’s sell-out to the actual downstream final product shipments are still large, given the pre-mentioned slow shipments of GB200 YTD, demand uncertainties associated with the roadmap and design changes, and rising macro risks.

On nVidia’s CoWoS orders (L+S) to TSMC, we pre-emptively lower our assumptions by 10-15% for 2025/2026F. Given the long lead time of foundry+CoWoS (e.g. almost five months) and HBM (likely six months) and the contracts signed between nVidia and HBM vendors, a big cut for CoWoS in 2025F could be tough. Given there is still gap between Blackwell supply and demand, we do not rule out the possibility that nVidia would continue cutting more CoWoS production plan in 2H25F in the coming months. The end demand by then is critical to watch. If the customers’ (such as CSPs) demand remains there and downstream can finally ramp up the system volume, we think the gap between Blackwell supply and demand could be narrowed by late-2025F.

In our model (Fig. 1 ) , we capture the discrepancy between different layers of nVidia AI server supply chain, from chips, to modules, and to the final racks. 

• For the upstream CoWoS-based chip supply, we cut our estimates on the supply of CoWoS-based GPUs for nVidia to 6.4mn/6.7mn units in 2025/26F (vs prior 6.9mn/7.9mn units in 2025/26F). We cut our CoWoS output assumptions for 2H25 to reflect the above-mentioned nVidia cut in March, and we further cut our estimates for 2026F, considering the rising Blackwell inventory level that would accumulate throughout 2025. 

• However, on the demand side (nVidia’s sell-in to ODMs or end customers), we estimate only 4.4mn/4.5mn units of nVidia GPUs are made into modules for final products in 2025/26F. There is also a major gap between the ideal GB rack number (e.g. 41.5k GB racks in 2025F) and the final GB rack shipments (20k GB racks in 2025F), and the gap (around 52%) is due to the yield loss of GB, slow production throughput of GB racks, and/or the buffer required for the complex coordination of the GB supply chain and after-market product warranty.

• We assume the combined gap from nVidia’s IC production to final GB rack output would reach 55% in 2025F, if we consider HGX is fully sold out. However, as we do not see a clear demand for HGX, this suggests that the gap could be wider than 55%. 

ASIC (application-specific integrated circuit) AI – relatively stable 

For AI ASIC, we have earlier highlighted the potential product transition of AWS (AMZN US, Not rated) in 4Q25F from Trainium 2 to Trainium 3. AWS also lowered its CoWoS in end-Feb, likely to remove overbooking. Since then, we think investor expectations have dropped from overly bullish level (2mn units of Trainium 2 in 2025E) to currently more realistic level (1.2mn units in 2025E).

However, we note that Trainium 2 will likely extend its life-cycle to 1H26F, from the earlier plan of a sharp production ramp-down by end-2025, likely because the slightly later ramp-up of Trainium 3 (which echoes our semi team’s view, as the earlier target of ramping up production by end-4Q25 was too aggressive and it usually takes a year from tape-out (1Q25) to IC mass production, not to mention another 1-2 quarters for rack qualification) For the Trainium 2 downstream supply chain, we observe a strong production ramp-up from late-Feb to March, after most of the bottlenecks were overcome. As downstream makers were constrained previously, after ramping up production in March, we believe volume throughout in 2025F will likely sustain at March levels. Upstream Trainium 2 suppliers were expected to have peak output in mid-2025, in our view, but given the potential substrate constraint, we also see a smoother production ramp-up and ramp-down in 1H25 and 2H25, respectively. More importantly, the upstream IC production and downstream production plan can match each other, unlike nVidia which has a notable gap.

For Google’s (GOOGL US, not rated) TPU, the next-gen TPU from Broadcom is likely to ramp up production from 2Q25F, with increased volumes in 2H25F. For Meta’s (META US, not rated) next AI ASIC, we observe Broadcom will ramp up a more meaningful volume by the end of 2025F, which could be the first ASIC of Meta with meaningful shipment volume.

Investment view: nVidia’s downstream names and AI ASIC plays look attractive in terms of valuation, as market expectations have been low 

Consistent with our view in Feb , we continue to prefer nVidia’s downstream names and AI ASIC plays over nVidia’s upstream names, because we think the low shipments of GB200 racks in 1H25 are fully expected by investors (investors sometimes are more conservative than us), and investor expectations on AWS ASIC are also becoming realistic, in our view. Since the global stock market sell-off in early April, weighed down by Trump’s new tariff policy, valuations of many AI server downstream ODMs have declined to 9-13x 2025E P/E (based on our/Bloomberg consensus estimates) (from 13-20x), and AI server downstream component makers’ valuations have dipped to 11-17x (from 15- 25x). We think these valuations are attractive, because server should be less impacted by the tariff policy, in our view. We think it is easier for the server supply chain to mitigate the tariff impact. The tariff-driven pricing pressure on the supply chain should also be lower than that on consumer products, given the supply chain’s B2B business and high-value but low-volume nature.

We reiterate Buy on Wiwynn (6669 TT, an AWS ASIC play), Wistron (3231 TT, an nVidia module, with upside in GB system), Quanta (2382 TT, a leading GB system ODM with diversified CSP customers), and Hon Hai (2317 TT, a leading GB system and nVidia module ODM). 

The GB300 design change, a return to the Bianca architecture, will benefit original Bianca suppliers such as HDI maker Unimicron (3037 TT, Buy), in our view, but the early beneficiaries of Cordelia architecture, such as socket makers, might be negatively impacted. However, we think the share price correction of Lotes (3533 TT, Buy) is overdone, as it is not yet qualified for nVidia’s GPU socket (i.e. nothing to lose in GB300) and it still has an opportunity to pursue the GPU socket market in terms of Vera Rubin generation.

In our view, the valuations of several high-quality component makers are also attractive, such as Delta (2308 TT, Buy), AVC (3017 TT, Buy), EMC (2383 TT, Buy), and Bizlink (3665 TT, Buy; link , covered by Kenny Chen; a major beneficiary from growing power density in server racks and the rising penetration of active electrical cable (AEC) deployed in both GPU and ASIC-based AI servers). We think the rising power wattage for AI, more powerful thermal solutions, lower-loss, higher-speed transmission materials, and higher speed, higher power cables are all secular growing trends for AI in the long run. We think current share price corrections offer good entry points for long-term investors to invest in these sector leaders.

On the upstream side, we have adopted a more cautious stance on AI semi since the end of 2024 (AI semi anchor ), with a contrarian rating downgrade of ASPEED (5274 TT, report ) and initiation of coverage on KYEC with a Neutral rating (2449 TT, report ). We expect their share prices to track nVidia’s supply chain sentiment (e.g. short-term upside catalyst from GB200/300 rack shipment bottoming out — if the momentum can be strong). One significant reason behind our cautious mid-term AI semi view from end of 2024 is that CoWoS would likely face an over-supply risk; we also note that some equipment orders for CoWoS capacity expansion after 2Q25F have been halted.

We still prefer TSMC and Alchip (3661 TT, Buy) in AI semi, despite TSMC’s recent overhang (geopolitical pressures and our below-consensus view on AI semi growth into 2026) and our view that Alchip’s Trainium 3 chip ramp-up momentum could be later than the company had earlier anticipated (end-2025). We have been of the view that the target of ramping up production by end-4Q25 was too aggressive as it usually takes a year from tape-out (1Q25) to IC mass production, not to mention another 1-2 quarters of rack qualification.

Xi Jinping Doesn’t Flinch at Trump—Why? Seoul Economic [Kang Haeryeong’s High-Tech]

Hello, readers with a keen interest in the information technology (IT) market. The keyword for this first half of the year is undoubtedly “tariffs.” You must be having a real headache over the trade risks unleashed by Trump’s administration.

Donald Trump’s ultimate target is Xi Jinping, the head of the “G2.” Starting his new term, Trump seems determined to slap tariffs on every product bearing the “Made in China” label. The White House even announced that cumulative tariff rates on certain Chinese exports have reached as high as 245%, unleashing a merciless tariff barrage.

But there’s a clear difference from Trump’s first term five years ago: China no longer cringes before the United States.

This phenomenon is even more evident in the semiconductor sector. As U.S.-origin semiconductor risks grew, China retaliated with its own semiconductor tariffs—an eye-for-an-eye approach. It hiked tariffs on certain U.S. semiconductor products from 84% to 125%, shaking U.S. industry to its core before eventually lifting them. (Memory semiconductors, however, still face retaliatory tariffs.)

Many people are surprised by how events have unfolded. Perhaps the most surprised of all is President Trump himself. Five years ago, China trembled at a single word from him—so why does it no longer waver in the face of a major punch?

From here, let’s examine China’s semiconductor industry situation to see what weapons Xi Jinping holds, and then summarize the message China is sending to Korea’s semiconductor ecosystem.

“Trump, It Might Be Time to Show Your Mettle Even in Materials, Parts, and Equipment” in Xi Jinping’s Mind

First, let’s take stock of China’s overall semiconductor ecosystem. Consider Morgan Stanley’s chart on China’s semiconductor self-sufficiency rate. Comparing late 2020—at the end of Trump’s first term—with 2025 is fascinating. China’s pace of semiconductor localization has been nothing short of transformative.

In particular, the equipment sector stands out. In 2020, domestic equipment accounted for only 5% of local use; in just five years, that rate has jumped 16 percentage points to 21%.

This rise is attributed not only to China’s top equipment maker, Naura, but also to firms like AMEC aggressively localizing equipment. I’ll delve more into Naura later.

China is charging full steam ahead to establish semiconductor equipment technology. A notable insight from recent reporting: if you strip away the casing of U.S.-made equipment on a Chinese production line, you’ll find that almost all the components inside are Chinese-made.

Two messages emerge from this. First, China is focusing more on “acquiring technology” (to put it positively) than on whether it infringes on U.S. equipment suppliers’ IP. Second, local component manufacturing has matured enough to actually run the equipment.

Here’s another insider tidbit: reports indicate that China has begun to stop importing U.S. semiconductor equipment. Multiple indications pointed to this, and U.S. export statistics confirm it: from around Q4 last year through February this year, exports of semiconductor equipment to China plummeted. Whether this reflects China’s rapid localization or is part of a broader strategy to check the U.S. remains to be seen, but it’s certainly intriguing data.

Growth in EDA tools—essential for semiconductor design—is likewise remarkable, up ten percentage points in five years. When we think of EDA tools, we picture U.S. brands like Cadence, Synopsys, and Siemens. Yet industry consensus now holds that Chinese EDA tools are “quite usable”: Primarius, Xpeedic, and Empyrean are frequently mentioned. One industry insider noted, “Primarius even pitches to Korean semiconductor design firms, and while it can’t match U.S. companies, it’s evaluated as ‘quite serviceable.’”

And the share of memory supply—especially NAND flash—has surged. Its ratio has risen by 23 percentage points in five years, thanks to YMTC’s growth. Industry voices warn that Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix should be more concerned about YMTC’s rising profile in NAND than about DRAM. As high-capacity servers increasingly use YMTC chips, Samsung and SK Hynix’s foothold in China is narrowing.

This explains why memory semiconductors aren’t included among China’s tariff-relief targets. Local players like YMTC are flooding the domestic market, and Samsung and SK Hynix maintain factories in Wuxi and Xi’an. In short, China’s calculation seems to be: “We can handle memory even without U.S. Micron.”

According to Morgan Stanley’s analysis, China’s CPU self-sufficiency remains below 10%, and its GPU self-sufficiency—crucial for AI chips—is at 0%. Just as Trump regulated exports of Nvidia’s H20, future measures will likely tighten AI chip and HBM memory transactions, targeting China’s Achilles’ heel. Whether Chinese firms can localize these critical components under U.S. pressure will determine the next phase of the battle.

While China Has Been Growing… What Has Korea Been Doing?

The core message of this article is simple: Xi Jinping isn’t intimidated by Trump because China has built confidence and conviction through solid inputs, making the outputs feel within reach. This line of thought carries a strong message for Korea’s semiconductor ecosystem.

Let’s shift the lens to Korea. On the surface, K-semiconductors are in a dominant position. Samsung still reigns supreme in production capacity, and SK Hynix posted record quarterly earnings in Q4 last year thanks to HBM, looking to have weathered tariff risks admirably. Yet drop just one tier below Samsung and SK Hynix, and it becomes clear that Korea is neither on par with nor even a match for China.

Recall Naura: China’s No. 1 equipment maker. You might dismiss it as a peripheral player from a technologically backward country. But compare it to Korea’s leading equipment firm, SEMES. Over the past five years, SEMES’s revenue has been stuck in the 2 trillion KRW range, with volatile operating profits. Naura, on the other hand, has been growing vigorously every year. Since 2022, its sales and operating profits began to outpace SEMES, and in 2023 and 2024 it widened the gap dramatically, earning a place among the global semiconductor equipment elite—likely ranking sixth after Applied Materials, ASML, Tokyo Electron, Lam Research, and KLA.

This contrast epitomizes the mood in the materials-parts-equipment (MPE) sectors of Korea and China. From major chipmakers like YMTC, CXMT, and SMIC to the very foundations of semiconductor manufacturing, China has invested across the board—and when it invests aggressively, it quickly gains competitiveness.

By 2019, China was still a peripheral player in semiconductors; today, it can throw a jab at the U.S. thanks to its government’s exceptionally bold support. The third-phase semiconductor fund, launched in June last year, tops the combined value of Phase 1 (~20 trillion KRW) and Phase 2 (~40 trillion KRW) at 69 trillion KRW (¥3440 billion). Unlike loans or tax credits, this fund delivers direct subsidies—real firepower. China’s pursuit of EUV equipment development is not something to scoff at.

Korea has also seen calls to fix its distorted semiconductor ecosystem. During the 2019 Japan export restrictions crisis, “MPE self-reliance” was a rallying cry. Yet six years on, Korea’s MPE weakness remains unaddressed.

According to the government, Korea’s MPE import dependence has hovered around 70% for years. Seventy percent of equipment in Samsung and SK semiconductor fabs is foreign-made—a severe handicap in the global semiconductor arms race. The equipment sector has run a trade deficit since 2005—21 consecutive years. Silicon wafers, the bedrock of semiconductors, have run a trade deficit for about 50 years since 1970. Domestic player SK Siltron alone can’t compete with advanced firms like Shin-Etsu and SUMCO.

This month, the Korean government announced it would increase planned fiscal investment in semiconductors from 26 trillion KRW through 2027 to 33 trillion KRW, allocating 21.6 trillion KRW for MPE support. The plan includes supporting 30–50% of new investment costs for MPE firms, capped at 15 billion KRW per project and 20 billion KRW per company. Yet industry opinion deems this woefully insufficient given the technology gap with major foreign firms and the need for tailored corporate support.

What the government is “scraping together” now feels like temporary pandemic relief funds rather than the direct subsidies China provides. To inject real cash into companies’ pockets, Korea needs a “Semiconductor Special Act”—but its passage remains murky.

In December of the year before last, the government held an “Industrial Supply Chain Strategy Meeting” and set a goal to reduce import dependence on key items from 70% to below 50% by 2030. A “Supply Chain Stabilization Program” was slated for announcement in June, but with domestic political turbulence and an unexpected presidential election season, there are fears it may fizzle out.

On April 27, Lee Jae-myung, the Democratic Party’s presidential candidate, visited SK Hynix in Icheon for a “K-Semiconductor” roundtable with industry leaders. While admiring top-tier technologies like HBM and state-of-the-art fabs is certainly a source of pride, it would have been valuable had he also considered the origin ratios of equipment inside those fabs and reflected on Korea’s stagnant MPE competitiveness versus China’s aggressively growing model.

BofA) Expert Call with Former Intel Lithography and Foundry Executive

Yesterday, we hosted an expert call with Klaus Shuegraf, currently VP at Photonic and formerly Director of Lithography Sourcing and VP of Foundry Strategy & Planning at Intel.

1. EUV Source Power and Increasing Lithographic Intensity Expected to Continue

Shuegraf acknowledged that the transition from N3 to N2 nodes does not significantly shrink feature sizes due to the Gate-All-Around (GAA) structure. However, he projected that lithographic intensity will continue to increase for nodes beyond that. He expressed confidence in ASML achieving 1000W source power from the current 600W, but noted that reaching 1500W would approach technical limitations.

2. 18A Node Outlook and High-NA Adoption Timing

In line with industry trends, Shuegraf stated that Intel must first prove the viability of its 18A node through its own products before attracting potential customers such as AVGO (Broadcom), NVDA (Nvidia), and AAPL (Apple M-series). He predicted that 2026 would be the mainstream ramp-up period for 18A, which would be about one year behind TSMC’s 2nm node production schedule. Regarding High-NA EUV, he noted that TSMC’s full adoption would likely be in the late 2020s, as it will take time for ASML to scale up production capacity.

3. Potential Expansion of EUV Adoption in DRAM

Shuegraf suggested that if leading HBM suppliers adopt EUV, it could drive broader EUV adoption across the DRAM industry. This is due to trends such as AI PCs and advanced packaging making DRAM a more specialized, rather than purely commoditized, product segment. While some customers may be able to maintain current lithographic intensity levels through 4F2 architecture, others are expected to adopt additional litho layers alongside 4F2.

4. Additional Notes on China and ALD

(A) Regarding China’s development of EUV using DPP (Discharge Produced Plasma), Shuegraf acknowledged that for AI use cases, high wafer throughput is not always essential. However, he commented that DPP is economically inefficient and presents challenges in supply availability.

(B) On the topic of ALD (Atomic Layer Deposition), he emphasized that ASMI remains the leading player due to its position as the only vertically integrated vendor with an in-house chemical supply chain.

Semiconductor Equipment / Foundry: Marginal Improvement in Industry Sentiment
 JP Morgan (J. Kwon, May 20, 2025)

1QCY25 results and outlook indicate that as chip stacking and process node evolution continues, demand for testing high-performance memory such as HBM (High Bandwidth Memory) and DDR5 is rising sharply. This is driving stable to mid-single-digit growth in both front-end and back-end testing and wafer fabrication equipment (WFE) markets. While the WFE market is projected to reach approximately $100 billion for the full year 2025 with a broadly optimistic outlook for 2026, macroeconomic and geopolitical uncertainties—especially tariffs—in 2H25 remain key concerns. We prefer Samsung Electronics (SEC), SK Hynix, Tokyo Electron, Advantest, and Hanmi to capture long-term structural opportunities.

• WFE Market: Solid Growth Momentum

• Leading manufacturers forecast the 2025 WFE market at $99–110 billion, indicating stable to mid-single-digit growth.

• Leading equipment vendors (LAM, KLA) are optimistic about continued adoption by leading foundries and logic fabs. Tokyo Electron expects double-digit growth in 2026.

• DRAM and NAND together are projected to account for around 35% of WFE demand, with DRAM growing to 20% due to HBM and DDR5 transitions, and NAND reaching 10%.

• HBM and Substrate Testing Ramping Up

• Front-end equipment suppliers like KLA and TEL classify HBM as a testing-intensive technology, benefiting from increased stacking layers and stricter quality control.

• Back-end testing equipment vendors (Advantest, Hanmi) report a significant increase in demand for HBM-related tools, with orders expected to continue releasing through 2H25.

• Applied Materials forecasts over 40% YoY revenue growth from HBM and DDR5 customers in 2025, reflecting surging demand for high-value-added memory process equipment.

• DRAM Technology Evolution Drives Equipment Refresh

• ASML is promoting broader use of EUV to simplify DRAM multi-patterning to single exposure, improving efficiency and output.

• LAM Research (LRCX) has made breakthroughs in etch technology, with its Akara system adopted for critical applications by major DRAM makers.

• ASMI sees increased demand for ALD and epitaxy tools due to high-k metal gate processes and future 4F² or vertical channel transistor adoption.

• NAND Demand Driven by Technology Transition

• LRCX’s ALTUS Halo system advances atomic layer deposition (ALD) for 3D NAND inter-layer technology, enabling low-resistance interconnects for 256+ layers.

• 3xx/4xx-layer NAND processes are expected to be adopted gradually over the next 3–5 years, driving a new round of equipment upgrades.

• Tokyo Electron has secured new orders in NAND channel etch and low-temperature dry etch, expecting 2026 NAND investments to focus on brownfield upgrades and capacity enhancement.

• Macro and Tariff Risk Mitigation

• While direct tariff impact is limited, the industry is closely watching potential disruptions to end-customer purchasing patterns and CapEx decisions.

• Major equipment vendors are strengthening supply chain diversification and regionalization to improve geopolitical risk resilience.

• Test equipment vendors like Advantest and Teradyne state that HPC and AI markets are relatively insulated from tariffs but continue to monitor macro demand shifts closely.

• China Market Developments
• China contributed 27% of total sales in 1Q25, down from 38% in 2024. ASML remains most optimistic, forecasting over 25% of its sales from China.

• LRCX, KLA, and AMAT all reported reduced spending in China on DRAM and mature logic nodes, though capacity build-out continues for 28nm and above.

• ASMI reported strong margins in China, and Teradyne saw a slight increase in local customer share. Overall demand in the China market is expected to gradually stabilize.

• Investment Recommendations and Catalysts

• We maintain an Overweight rating on Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, as valuation risks are low and fundamentals are expected to improve.

• In the SPE (semiconductor production equipment) sector, we prefer Advantest and Tokyo Electron, which are set to benefit from equipment growth driven by HBM, DDR5, and 3D NAND technologies.

• Medium-term catalysts include:
1. Progress in 2026 equipment order negotiations among major manufacturers,
2. Tariff resolution developments, and
3. Expansion of AI accelerated computing demand.

Industry commentary supports durability throughout 2027.

I've always been bullish on memory with $MU / Samsung / solana:SKHYhSjuRWHgikq8eRKbtBbpABgJSkd7ytQV14i9EQ3 for the 2026-2027 period.  

Same opinion, even after $NVDA call. 

And I've been fervently defending how high end memory demand is structural + OP for operating income (especially during Iran tensions around LNG/Helium). 

Nvidia earnings just reaffirms what we know about extreme demand since commitments went from $119B -> $279B largely driven by memory procurement. 

Nvidia's CFO also said: "We are experiencing extreme pricing conditions in memory."

As for what I've done, H1 2026 I was extremely overweight in memory: 

With $MU, $SNDK, Phison, $SIMO, Nanya, Macronix, Winbond, and $EWY / SK Hynix (HBM/DRAM + NAND + legacy DRAM/NAND + controllers + NOR Flash).

I trimmed down those positions aside from Samsung/SK Hynix longs, since I do believe many have been rerated (eg. Micron $300 -> $1000+ already).

I think the largest price discovery period has played out, but just a waiting game for the operating income to catch up (esp u samsung)

And I used that period to go overweight on photonics. 

But I do believe we're seeing a relatively newer cascade down into the "legacy legacy" memory like DDR2/DDR3 with the "legacy" players like Winbond leaving some of those segments.  

Where the price hikes finally hit the 40-60% Q/Q mark, which reminds me of the extreme $SNDK days, across  DDR2/DDR3.  

Which is why I started up positions in ESMT (1.9x P/E from July annualized) and Etron. 

Maybe we'll see a price discovery moment further down the legacy memory stack (could be wrong), but that's the area I've focused on recently.

earlier_mentions.raw_text:
Winbond is actually withdrawing from DDR2 to focus on DDR4/DDR3 and said they expect 2027 to be even tighter. 

They're beginning capacity discussions for 2029-2030 + moving toward higher end, so don't quite see them having much to allocate toward older lines again. 

As for other players moving toward older lines, qualification takes a lot of time... and there's just very low incentive to. 

I looked for foundry dependence, PSMC is Taiwanese, so all good geopolitically. 

As for wafer allocations, if I had to put my supply chain hat resiliency hat on, if ESMT stopped supplying DDR2, it would just be absolute destruction downstream, so don't see that scenario (since they're probably the world's largest merchant supplier for this line if Winbond exits)

So don't quite think it would happen... but if they get less wafer allocations, the ASP just gets hiked even more, so earnings would likely remain strong.

Rant: this $CRCL chart is a great lesson on why TA means very little - fundamentals matter more.

When people were posting $BULL TA's at IPO, I was doing arbitrage between warrants and rolling my eyes. 

BULL went from $10 to $70+ but people were trading on 1% of float. When shares were unlocked, BULL went back to $10 IPO price.

For CRCL, we saw the rally from $31 IPO price to $200+ because people are trading on a limited float and MC was almost the same as $COIN. (which has 50% interest revenue sharing with Circle on top of their crypto exchange)

When 1.4m+ Circle shares had early unlock, the price crashed back down to $130.  If you ever see $CRCL at $200, it's an easy short Circle long Coinbaes play. 

The full 180 day lock up is December 2nd and you have another $10B+ USD of potential selling pressure in two months.  

I am bullish on USDC and Circle/Coin but with the existing business model it doesn't make sense that $CRCL should ever be worth more than 1/2 of $COIN today at $200 given how Stablecoin businesses like Tether make money off interest income. 

TA doesn't mean anything with upcoming share lockups.

Lesson: Float & fundamentals > lines on a chart.

1/ Rate cuts don’t nuke earnings. Virtu’s term loans are floating (financing +2.5%). total $1.545B. −75 bps ≈ ~12M yr interest savings (not all funding prices down but most are floating tho)

2/ Using Q2 as an anchor (EPS $1.65 / adj $1.53; NI ~$293M; rev ~44% YoY).

If we est EPS 10–12% for lower VIX + ~2.6% for net rate drag -> $1.31–$1.34 EPS/qtr -> $5.22–$5.35 next 12 months

$35.21 / $5.35 = 6.58x forward p/e
$35.21 / $5.22 = 6.74x forward p/e

Even if we overshoot because of good Q2 quarter as an anchor without rate cuts, EPS $4.78 -> 7.4× forward p/e, is still extremely good.  

Other websites like Value Investing estimate forward p/e to be 6.99 - 8 forward p/e. 

3/ There's ~$303M authorization remaining for buybacks off a small 5.2B marketcap.  

If vol normalizes or spikes, expect both EPS and the multiple to lift from today’s ~6–7×. If not, it's undervalued and you can sit back with buybacks. 

IN my opinion Virtu is a great asymmetrical hedge. If VIX stays low and we get rate cuts, VIRT is undervalued + goes up anyway or stays flat/slightly down, other equities go up, and it serves its hedging case. The Nov 2025 market-structure changes probably is the larger risk to payment order flow, which might create some headwind. 

Regardless VIX increases and other equities go down, VIRT would get re-rated and goes up.  

I just see risk/reward being good at these levels so bought Calls. Would recommend shares instead.

Use this opportunity to buy stocks on dips. Historically  initially, stocks drop on the news but ends up increasing new the tail end (eg. Oct 2021 (Debt Ceiling) 15 days, SPY +1.34%).

(eg. growth stocks that rely on forward earnings, stuff like Zillow or others that benefit from increased housing sales from lower rates, or small cap stocks with floating interest debt cut).

But we'll likely get rate cut frontrunning in Oct after the short lived gov shutdown drop (if there is any)

3. SEASONALITY TAILWIND. October (front-running) -> November -> December. Huge opportunity for stocks.

E-Commerce like $AMZN, tech like $APPL retail like $LULU, etc. All benefit from seasonality such as Christmas shopping, Nov black friday deals.

Tech also performs great in December, so if you're position you can leverage longs aiming for March, on a government rate shutdown dip and just ride the wave until Jan.

I don't know how how it's going to play out exactly, but just going off assumption that stocks drop off confirmation fears, it's likely short term and a great time to build long positions, not sell, because of macro + seasonality tailwind + immateriality of government shutdowns historically.

So people keep asking me about $RBRK almost every other post and I know it's really popular on X. 

I ended up looking into it so people stop asking (and added some Rubrik to my portfolio at $82). 

TLDR my own research:

- Cybersecurity company (industry trades at extremely high multiples, look at $CRWD or $NET)

- 80% gross margins (great)

- $1B+ ARR, grew 40-50% Y/Y (great)

(comparison to NET, ~2.2B+ ARR, growing 22% Y/Y, almost 5x the MC)

- OpEx spend: 60-75% of revenue goes to marketing. This is a huge positive. 

OpEx marketing spend is great but it looks really bad short term eg. $HOOD when they give customers 3% to transfer, it hurts short term in earnings reports bc it's deceptive and not many people do the breakdown but long term when they cut back on spend, customers are sticky and this helps a lot with profitability. 

FCF was positive, but breakdown of opex expenses was mainly marketing, which is a good thing, unlike Snapchat google cloud opex.

- Diversified client base like Cloudflare (eg. goldman, pepsi, accenture, etc).

Downsides:

- Balance sheet not the best, $1.1B debt or so to fund acquisitions. At least it's about acquisitions.

- Don't like how their forward revenue numbers slowed down 20-25% compared to something like $NBIS growing like 700% or something more for next year. Obviously unfair comparison, but that's why I liked Neoclouds more. 

_

Looks like a good mid term hold with a pretty simple plan -> scale customer base -> scale back marketing + sticky base -> catch up to industry multiples in cybersecurity and hv higher FCF.

Usually these types of growth companies with high gross margins (eg. $HOOD back at $18, growing ~50 y/y) that turn profitable, re-rate the hardest.

$RBRK just gotta spend less on marketing down the road and suddenly they have a lot of fcf with their sticky customer base.

TLDR: Great buy for cybersecurity sector, better opportunities elsewhere.
